utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Waespi, may I just say that the Chamber will be issuing later today the schedule relating to the Fridays, how we will treat Fridays. Some Fridays we will sit a full day, from 9.00 until 5.00; some Fridays we'll sit a half day, from 9.00 until 1.00 or 1.30; and some Fridays we will not sit at all. Now, tomorrow, is a Friday when, according to the schedule we have elaborated, we will sit a full day. But I'm, of course, aware that on the schedule that was issued originally, we were down to sit a normal day, which is a half day on Friday. So I hope this will not inconvenience any of the parties, that is sitting tomorrow a full day. It may that be we can stop at 4.30. I see Mr. Tapuskovic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I understand this and I see the reasoning behind it, and we have to use every working day we have. But I wanted to visit the accused in the detention unit after the hearing tomorrow because of the witnesses who have already arrived, in order to be able to discuss what is ahead with the accused. And Friday was our only option to go there to the detention unit, and I wanted to go there straight from the courtroom to discuss the witnesses who are already here, to just to do some essential discussion, consultations with him. I will, of course, abide by your decision, but this is a situation that we in the Defence are facing. It is difficult for us to do all our duties in the defence of our client, and I really have to communicate and consult with my client. I don't see how I will be able to examine the witnesses if I can't consult with him before that, and I wanted to go to see him straight from the courtroom, and the problem is that we can't do that over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It is not possible to do that today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have three witnesses here. It's difficult to explain, and the fourth one is in fact arriving today. So this is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm, of course, very sensitive to the issue raised by Mr. Tapuskovic, and we take that into consideration. So that, in principle, we will not sit in the afternoon tomorrow. But, Mr. Tapuskovic, if we find that we need, say, another hour, if we find that we need another hour to finish a witness tomorrow, I hope that we would be able to reorganise the schedule a little. Would that still present a difficulty for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because of the house rules in the detention unit, I have to be there by 3.00, quarter to 3.00. I have to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will not sit in the afternoon. All right. Let's proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veljovic. Let's return to the document we finished off with yesterday --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- which was P694. Do you remember having looked at the first page of this document, Mr. Veljovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is it the document again on your screen. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you weren't sure who signed the document, or you wanted to see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if we could please go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you accept, looking at the first page which is still there, it talks about quite a number of troops that were to be assembled from various units. I think it was all together more than 10.000 troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We can go back to the first page later. Well, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have a look again, Witness. Do you see that it talks about quite a number of troops to be used in this operation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last page now. Now can you tell us who signed this order?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Major-General Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you look at these two initials - I'm sorry - if you look at the two initials just to the left of the signature, it is GS and MG. In your opinion, what does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MG would be the typist, and CS that would be the person who actually dictated the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was CS? Was that Cedo Sladoje, the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that's the initial of Cedo Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. So you accept that this is a valid order?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes,, it's a valid order. In light of the heading and everything, I attested this document is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next document which talks about this Operation Lukovac 95. This document was 23rd March. Now, we go into 4th April, so a few days later, and this is exhibit 696, please. And looking at it, can you tell us what it is, Witness?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SRK command, strictly confidential, number 20/04-115, 4th, April, 1995, order for artillery number 1/95.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it again relates to the Operation Lukovac 95, as you can see at the top on the right side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you go down to item number 3, you see that among the weaponry used by the corps artillery group are two aerial bomb launchers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what item, what number? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was item number 3.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see here the corps artillery group, comprising the Howitzer battery, 122-millimetre -- 122-millimetre was the self-propelled Howitzer battery, 130-millimetre cannon, 128-millimetre plumb and multiple rocket launcher, 128-millimetre Oganj, VBR, two aerial bomb launchers will provide support to the forces at the point of the main defence effort. So this is not an attack. This is not a offensive action, but a defensive action, and there you have the commander of the group is the artillery battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And if we go to the next page, we see the person who authorised or signed this document, and this is again Major-General Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it here. No, no. There is no signature here. There's just a stamp at least here in front of me, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just move on to the last page, which is the third page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness said that this is not an attack; this is a defensive action.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I wanted to ask the witness what aspects of that order indicate its defensive character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To prepare the artillery, in case of an attack by the 1st Corps forces, then the artillery should be ready to target the personnel and the firing points, materiel, equipment used in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it was essentially an order requiring the preparation of the artillery in the event of an attack by the 1st Corps forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we see here in this document that the commander was prepared to use air bombs. Now, you have told us, I believe two days ago, that you often heard commanders complain that the weapons shouldn't be used because of the safety of your own troops. Did you remember testifying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "commanders," you mean commanders of the SRK, subordinate SRK units?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if we move -- and I think you also told us -- and while you were answering that question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If P511 could be retrieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also told us that some brigades possessed air bombs and others didn't. Do you remember telling us that two days ago?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that they had air bomb launchers, and I don't know where they took the air bombs from, what storage facilities, because the air bombs were manufactured, as far as I know, in an area controlled by the Muslim forces, Bugojno, Travnik, something like that. And in our areas inhabited by Serbs and in the area of responsibility of the Republika Srpska army, there were no production facilities for air bombs. And I said that launchers were made just by ordinary craftsmen. This was not done in a factory. This was an imperfect weapon that caused great risk for the crew. For our own forces, it is a very inaccurate weapon because bombs have to be dropped from the planes. That's what they're made of. I think I have already explained all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you did, and I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, can I just kick in a short question. Returning to the point that the President was raising just a while ago, I was wondering what the impact of the previous document really is. So if we can kindly go back to the previous document on page 1. Thank you for your patience. Because if you look at paragraph 2 or point number 2 in that document, as I recall, it also foresees a counter-attack against the enemy, and that doesn't seem to be to be particularly defensive. So I just wanted to clarify what is really the impact of this order for artillery. I understand the witness to say that this order was issued in order to prepare for the defence, but it seems to me that it also anticipates a counter-attack on the following axis, if you see on the last line of paragraph 2: Lupoc-Tunov Stan-Borilovac-Rakitnica and the Kozja Luka-Ogorelikuk axis. Is a counter-attack a normal part of a defence, is my question? I don't know whether you can clarify that, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are documents drafted by the brigade staff, and you can see from this, as I already explained yesterday, that sometimes the Chief of Staff and the commander of the corps have their own meetings, and they make decisions without informing the officers in the units, the commanding officers in the units. This is the usual practice in every army in the world. You have various variants for operations and not all of them are then implemented. The commander here specified that if the enemy attacks, there should be intense fire response here in this area between Bjelasnica and Treskavica. Ogorelikuk is a ridge connecting these two. And so if there is an attack, and if it is possible for our forces to launch a counter-attack, we then regain some of our previous positions. But this does not mean that an attack had been launched on their side, and that we actually responded. So we can plan for things that we never implement, because that is how it is done in the military, in the various staffs. You put various things on paper so that you have them in any eventuality, and that way you're ready at a given moment to perform your military tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can move back to P511, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Isn't that an example, Mr. Veljovic, for the possession of air bombs by one of the brigades as you had mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1st Ilidza Infantry Brigade Command, I already stated that it had a launcher, and it probably had the air bombs, as indicated here. The date was the 12th of June, 1995. That was when the offensive was under way, the offensive launched by the BH army, 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, If could document could be admitted. Previously, it has been marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is will be admitted as P511.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to also put to you that these air bombs were actually used. They were launched in Sarajevo; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those bombs were never launched to target the city area in view of their accuracy because the distances here are very small, especially here at Ilidza, Hrasnica, Butmir, because an air bomb could easily have hit our positions, our villages. This bomb is completely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is highly destructive; and if it hits an inhabited area, it causes great damage and a lot of casualties. And had it hit an inhabited any area there, would have been 50 or even 100 casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And as you just pointed out, Hrasnica was indeed an inhabited area.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Highly inhabited area. It borders with our Serb village, Bojkevic, which has about 850 houses. These are two settlements that are physically adjacent. They touch each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to hear there is an order by Commander Milosevic acknowledging that he actually launched an air bomb into the centre of Hrasnica, and this dates of 7th April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I said already that if that had been launched, the casualties would have been enormous. And as far as I know, at the time of the offensive or before the offensive in 1994, there were no such casualties coming from that type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If Exhibit P225 be prepared, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is a combat report by the SRK; is that correct, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, strictly confidential, number 20/04-1-103, the 7th of April -- or the 4th. The 7th of April, 1995. In April 1995, that's when there was a cease-fire and an exclusion zone for artillery weapons in a 20 kilometre diameter, all the way up to the 1st of May, 1995. All artillery weapons were under the control of the United Nations forces at check-points. I don't know at all how we could have taken our weapons out and carried this kind of action out, and seeing that this order is dated the 7th of April, 1995, when the cease-fire was signed a four-month cease-fire, on both sides. The civilian and the military authorities did that, and it was as far back as in December. I think that UNPROFOR would have reacted strongly to that, and that did not happen. Now, how this order came about? Was this just a preparatory thing or was -- or did one of the artillery men just draft this, and did the commander just sign it without knowing? Terrible sanctions would have ensued. We certainly would have been bombed had we tried to take four Howitzers from the check-point. I mean, in May, we were bombed by UN forces; and had we fired an air bomb, we would have suffered catastrophic losses inflicted by NATO aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the last page of this document. Can you tell us who authorised, who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was prepared by Milan Ugresic. The late Milan Ugresic, Mira, typed this out. He was the chief of anti-aircraft artillery. He was not in charge of land artillery at all. He was -- and it was signed by commander Major-General Dragomir Milosevic on the 7th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the second page of this document. Our forces, "Nasa Snaga." I learned that much. It says, does it not, "We responded to enemy fire as follows," and that of course goes to the Main Staff this document, this combat report. It says under 2: "In Ilidza, PBR 120-millimetre" --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilijas, Ilijas first. The Ilijas Infantry Brigade. The weapons are an anti-aircraft gun and an 82-millimetre recoilless gun, and then the Ilidza Infantry Brigade used a 120-millimetre mine, and one 250 kilogram AB was launched in the centre of Hrasnica. According to the interception centre, the Muslims claim that the luna rocket landed. That a rocket landed. Luna is an enormous land to land missile in the zone of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade; that is to say, on our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But going back to the first sentence, what General Milosevic tells here his superior command, the Main Staff is that "we responded by firing by launching a 150-kilogram air bomb at the centre of Hrasnica." That's what General Milosevic informs his superiors about; isn't that a fact.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is what this sentence says: "According to the interpretation centre, the Muslims claim that a luna rocket landed." A luna is a much bigger rocket. It's a land to land missile. It has a very big range, too. I don't know, it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That was the assessment of the Muslim who actually responded. Let's move to the next issue, and, Witnesses, you have been shown on Tuesday, I believe, a series of documents by the ABiH setting out all kinds of weaponry the ABiH had in their possession or used or deployed. And these documents were D190, D191, and D192, and so on. Do you remember having looked at the lists of these documents? I think, the orders came from the commander of the 12th ABiH Division, Mr. Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything here. Nothing's come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I can show you the documents again, if you want. I just ask you: Do you remember having been shown a series of documents created by the 1st Corps, indeed the command of the ABiH army? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 8th. I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me show you a document. That's fine. Let me show you D190, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be retrieved. If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this date. Is it the 8th of August or the 8th of June? I can't understand what it says exactly. If it is the 8th of August, I wasn't in the corps. If it's the 8th of June, I was in the corps. MR. WAESPI:

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me detach from these documents. You remember having been shown documents about weaponry, about arms that the ABiH had in defending the city of Sarajevo. Do you remember having seen all these documents about weaponry that the ABiH had?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what period?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In 1995 while you were operations officer in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I could not see and I could not know precisely in a war situation what the ABiH army had. Such documents about the forces and their deployment were submitted by the intelligence organ. It was for the artillery that here in this courtroom, I saw some documents when I spoke about tactical issues. That's when Mr. Tapuskovic asked me is that correct, is that correct, he showed me their map, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I am about to -- the documents you saw in this courtroom shown to you by the Defence counsel about the weaponry of the ABiH. You remember having seen these documents here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, among all these documents the Defence showed to you, perhaps during preparatory sessions, have you seen one single document which would show that the ABiH had air bombs and launchers to deploy these air bombs from? Have you seen any single document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I heard during the war from intelligence organs, especially in 1994 and 1995, that the Muslim forces imported from some country or manufactured air bombs of their own and that they had them. My lawyer never showed me such documents here, as far as air bombs are concerned, and not in his office either. While I was operations officer in the war, according to the intelligence organs, I heard that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had launchers and air bombs, and also that they had made something similar to the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was this intelligence organ who told that you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was Marko Luganja, intelligence organ; and Bukova, there were two of them; and a lieutenant. And they were involved in gathering this information. I don't know how they gathered it, so then it was reported verbally that the forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina already had launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when was it that Mr. Luganja told you that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that we discussed that sometime during the cease-fire, January, February, 1995. I don't know the exact date, but at any rate, at a particular briefing that is what was stated, that they had such equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And have you seen any evidence of such equipment? Have you seen any document which would prove that these weapons indeed existed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned that during the offensive, they launched a bomb at the TV headquarters, or rather, the TV of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was under the control of -- well, I don't know what happened. There was this explosion. Now, was it that bomb or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who told you that? Whom did you learn that from?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we found out about this from our colleagues, the operations men from the Ilidza Brigade. And an explosion was heard, a very strong explosion, because we had a forward command post in Vogosca, and it's not that I saw it being fired or that I saw it land, I personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the only thing you know about this incident is that you heard the explosion.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a strong explosion. Because when a powerful thing like that explodes, you hear it hundreds of kilometres away, let alone right there, five or six or seven or ten kilometres away. And I did not see the mushroom going up, because I had the hill of Zuc in front of me, sheltering me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, that's correct, many people heard this powerful explosion. Indeed, UNPROFOR heard it and complained about this explosion to commander Dragomir Milosevic for having launched such an air bomb. Isn't that the fact that it was the SRK who had launched this air bomb into the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, Mr. Waespi. No. No. Not at the city, not at any cost. It's not only that it would fall on the Muslim positions but also our settlements like Nedzarici, Lukavica, Vojkovici, Grbavica, Vogosca. No. Who dared launch that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What if you knew that Commander Dragomir Milosevic congratulated his troops for the launching of this air bomb on to the TV tower, which says was a location where lies, Muslim lies were spread? Isn't that an admission that Commander Dragomir Milosevic acknowledges that his troops have fired at the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see that. I'd like to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think, Mr. President, this document is on the list that I prepared, because that is an item I couldn't foresee. It was certainly not communicated in the 65 ter summary. I believe the exhibit is P42. With your leave, with leave of the Defence, I'd like to -- P42, I would like to show that to the witness since he would like to see that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be shown. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just want it to be known that the Defence agrees. Mr. Waespi asked whether the Defence agrees to this, and the Defence is not opposed to it but then you have decided already, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was my decision, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can we look at the top of it. It is an SRK document signed in Vogosca, 30th June, 1995, and it goes to all SRK units, and also to the SRK command, the IKM, which is the forward command post in Trnovo. Did you see that, Mr. Veljovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. It says: "Submit to the SRK command Trnovo, forward command post, to all SRK unit on the front line, the report on the situation at the front." Do you want to read it and then I'll answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's just move right to the centre, and the key parts where the TV tower is discussed is in the middle, where it says: "The Serbian soldiers are displaying unprecedented heroism, not letting the enemy get closer to their homes and families. The General Staff of the VRS commander Colonel-General Ratko Mladic commanded the heroism of units in the north-western part of the front, and numerous congratulations also arrived from unit commanders and civilian government institutions. "Our artillery forces are responded with precision to the Muslim artillery attacks. In one such response, on 28th June, they hit the BHRTC, radio television centre, the centre of media lies against the struggle of the Serbian people." Does that convince you that the SRK actually launched this shell, this bomb against the TV tower on the 23rd of June, Mr. Veljovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "artillery." That is a different thing from air bomb launchers. I read it properly, so it doesn't say here that an air bomb was launched. It says that the artillery had operated. The artillery has very small launchers, small projectiles; whereas, an air bomb is something completely different, 250 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Do you remember, maybe a half an hour ago, I showed the order of artillery, the plan of artillery in relation to offensive or defensive, whatever you can't to wall it, Operation Lukovac 95. And there it outlined all the artillery pieces, which you read out, and you not only talked about proper artillery assets, and I agree with you, but it was also included launches of air bombs, part of the artillery plan. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An air bomb launcher does not belong to guiding artillery fire. Artillery fire was invented by human beings thousands of years ago, and what is used here is some kind of mindless catapult, and that is not artillery. And in this paragraph, it says very nicely that it was artillery, as you say, and one artillery projectile of 100 or 155 millimetres. I mean, that is a big difference from 250 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Artillery was then responsible for firing the TV tower on 28th of June, 1995. Let's move on just one or two more topics. And the first topic I would like to raise with you is Defence Exhibit 186. Do you remember that, I think, yesterday you discussed a document - I think it was on Tuesday, in fact - dated 12th of August, 1995. And you were also asked a couple of questions by Judge Harhoff about this document, and you were asked specifically about page 2.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, this is not the time when I was in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the point I wanted to make. You can't really comment on the intentions the corps commander, Dragomir Milosevic, made at that time when he drafted this document. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I see here commander, Major-General Dragomir Milosevic. There is no signature. There is no signature on what I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you look at the typings, these initials just above the signature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: DM, UN. I don't know. DM, UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, usually, as you testified, the first two initials mark the person who authored it, who authorised, and the second one is the typist. You remember we had an example with Cedo Sladoje, the Chief of Staff, the initials of the Chief of Staff, CS in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Yes. Now this DM, is it DM or DN? It is a bit unclear. And is it UM?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I suggest it be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enlarge it, but there is something here, some kind of a signature here but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, since Dragomir Milosevic signed it, I suggest to you that it is DM, and I suggest to you it was Dragomir Milosevic who personally created, drafted this document; and then Mr. or Mrs. UM typed it. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He does not dictate a text. This is prepared and he just read it is; and if it says the commander, General Dragomir Milosevic, then he signs it his own hand. That means that he approve it is if I signs it in his own hand. But he doesn't draft the text, write the text are. I don't know who this is, DM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Because you weren't in the Corps Staff at that time, that is no issue. But it is an authentic document, is it not, if you look at the first page of the document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not signed by the commander, and it's not identical. If somebody signs for him, then it has to say "for," "za." And usually it is Cedo Sladoje. So in the corps he has to authorise people in terms of who can sign what. At this moment, I was not in the Corps Staff, and I don't know the answer to your question. I just see that this is not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But if you look at the -- the top of the document, you can see that it was apparently -- it is stamped by one of the subordinate battalions, the 4th Signal Battalion command. So you agree with me, it might have been in a telex version, that this document left the corps command and was processed by some unit outside the corps command. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commander of the SRK, forward command post, strictly confidential, the 12th of August, 1994, very urgent, bring the units to full combat readiness, order, deliver to the SRK command post, 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade, 4th Air Defence, Light Artillery Regiment, 4th Anti-tank Battalion, 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, Ilidza Infantry Brigade, 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. "Based on the information partially confirmed in the field and in order to prevent penetration, deblockade of the so-called BiH army forces from Sarajevo, I hereby order all units on the positions" -- "all units on the positions and in the regions of deployment around Sarajevo ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So having read all this information, do you accept that this is an authentic document that went out to at least one unit or was processed by at least one unit. Do you anticipate that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top part and everything else is in order, except for the missing signature, and I don't know if this can be acknowledged as an authentic document without a signature. I don't know what the purpose of this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And you were shown the document by the Defence first, and I just note that when the Defence discussed this document with you, in fact, elicited information from you about that document, you didn't raise any doubts about the authenticity of this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. Following from this document, you made a few comments when you were shown this document by the Defence, and you said that "The corps commander, General Milosevic," - and I quote you, because it is an important part of your evidence - "this was particularly stressed and reports were being sent to units saying that such buildings, the civilian population and roads and movements of people shall not be targeted at any cost, except on his specific orders, and he was the one not to ever issue such an order." And that's on page 5752, the transcript of Tuesday, two days ago. Do you remember having testified about that, and do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please -- please read it in entirety and then tell me what do you want me to specifically comment on, and then I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just want to have you confirm that you indeed said that on Tuesday, that General Milosevic stressed and that reports were being sent to units, that the city not be shelled, except on his specific orders, and he was the one not to ever issue such an order. That's what you said on Tuesday. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, an order meant that we were not allowed to fire at built-in areas, roads, and populated areas, only exceptionally on his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And by "his orders," you mean the orders of the corps commander, General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you give me one example of a staff meeting or another document which would show to the Trial Chamber, to us, of one instance when Dragomir Milosevic gave such an order or issued such a statement, that the city not be shelled? When was that said? When was that "stressed," as you say, by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were present here when we commented on the fact that the targets in the town shall not be targeted, and it is specifically emphasised cultural and historical monuments like Bascarsija, Vrbanja bridge, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I heard you. I just want an example of an instance when General Milosevic told subordinate units or told his Corps Staff about what he just said, that the city shouldn't be targeted? Just one date, if you an remember.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the commander's daily duty to issue warnings to the officers and commands. And when he went to see the soldiers in the trenches, he demanded that they do not target specifically populated area. In order to the to provoke the enemy, use fire against troops only if you are being shot at, and that was the real truth about the document sitting here in the courtroom. He was a man of high morale values and a professional, and I think that his personality is commendable. He was a compassionate person. There were children on both sides. There were friends and neighbours. We intermarried with Muslims and others. There were our people, thousands of our people in the city. Let us just look where the separation lines were. And when they were fired upon, maybe some outskirts areas were damaged, but these were already evacuated. I said this, and I don't think I have to repeat this for the umpteenth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No you don't have to. But I would like to hear an example when you say that you went to the trenches and commander Milosevic talked to the soldiers. Can you give us the location of one of those trenches where you were with General Milosevic and he talked to the soldiers. Give us the location of that part of the front line or within the front lines, I don't care, and if you remember the date. If you can't remember the date because it is too far away, that's okay. But if it happened on a repeated nature, perhaps you can recall one specific example of the commander talking to his soldiers and reminding them of their duties on the Geneva Convention, as you testified on Tuesday. One example, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, only when he went to the Main Staff or to some institutions with tasks and an order, it happened every day. Unless he was on leave, he went to inspect and see the units. He was the only corps commander who visited virtually every trench. This was supposed to be done by an operations officer, but, no, he was the one always in the field. I often accompanied him, not always, and he always underlined whenever he went there. Whether it was in December, whether it was in June, whether it was during the offensive, he always repeated the rules of warfare. "Gentlemen, comrades, soldiers," this is how he addressed them, "do not violate these rules and set an example just like the Serbian army always did. They shared the last piece of bread with their prisoners of war, and this is what Archibald Rice spoke about the Serbian army in the First World War. And this is what we have to spread around the world about the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why was it important to all the time on a -- on such an intensive rate talk to the soldiers to respect the rules of war if nothing happened, as you say? If the city was never shelled, if nothing happened to the civilians inside the city, why did Commander Milosevic have to all the time repeat it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't repeat it every day. He said it in one trench then in another trench; but as I said, that was always an instruction not to violate the rules because this will be followed by liability and responsibility. And this is what command officers are supposed to do because there are all various people in units. I said that yesterday, that there were very serious criminals serving long prison sentences in units. Only once was enough to go to the front line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Only going to the front line only once was not enough.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to go there on a regular basis and this is something that every army does. If we had an intention and had we fired --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Mr. President. I just wanted to mention something about the transcript. On Page 24, line 25, [In English] "There were very serious criminals serving long prison sentences in units." [Interpretation] That's the end of it, but in B/C/S, and I'm going repeat that and I'm asking you to please check. This is what he said: He said there were all kinds of profiles within the SRK, ranging from people who had been convicted for certain crimes to doctors, Ph.D.s. That's what the doctor said, and that changes -- what you find in the transcript changes what the witness said totally. That's the reason why I'm on my feet. I notice differences in the translation so far, but this is a very serious one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We note that correction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In view of this, can the witness kindly be asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Veljovic, there was a problem with interpretation just now, and it might have arisen because of the speed at which you are speaking. So would you speak a little more slowly and also into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you suggesting then -- I'm just asking you - you can say yes or no, clarify - that it was the criminals, these criminals who were released from prison, that were killing civilians inside the confrontation line in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Waespi. What I'm saying is that not -- had this not been brought to their attention every day or once in ten days, they could have made a mistake, and this was to be prevented and there were under constant surveillance of security organs. A man can drink a bottle of brandy and commit an incident, but you can't have a general behind every bush or and at every location and checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have now testified I don't know how many hours. I don't think you have ever mentioned the fact that civilians inside the confrontation line, Muslim, Serbs, other nationalities whoever was part of the civilian population in Sarajevo, was exposed to a campaign of sniping were killed, as civilians were killed by snipers, by shelling from outside. Do you accept that the civilian population in Sarajevo was terrorised, that they suffered tremendously. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So all these --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were isolated killings on our side as well, even of children, but everybody says by sniper. All rifles can kill at the front, not only snipers. There were two girls of ours who were killed in Grbavica. I didn't address the issue of civilians too much. I was more involved in tactical issues and day to day life of units. Probably you will have witnesses here whose mothers or close relatives were killed. I lost my own brother and other relatives. I could have found him a shelter somewhere. I was a victim myself. I was wounded. I lost my brother, I lost my relatives. My uncle's son and daughter, his wife is the only survivor. So if I'm going tell the Honours all these stories and fairy tales this is not my role in this courtroom. I'm just talking about a military aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So testimony of international observers, soldiers of UNPROFOR, United Nations, about the suffering of the population of any ethnicity in Sarajevo are fairy tales?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think accept that that is a reasonable question to put to the witness, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The testimony of UNPROFOR, other international observers about the suffering of the civilians inside Sarajevo during the time Dragomir Milosevic was the commander, all these testimonies about the suffering, do they -- do you accept them or you don't accept them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Waespi. Let me first explain this. We did not hold this under blockade as shown by this map. There were all supply lines of the whole town of the Sarajevo with 400.000 inhabitants were controlled by the Muslims. Our water sources were under our control. 75 per cent of Ilidza, Lukavica, Moscanica from the area of Hresa, from Radava in the Vogosca sector, not a single water source was under the Muslim control. They had plenty of water. Sometimes breakages happened, but that was something that happened in peacetime as well. Had that been the case, they wouldn't have a drop of water. One of the moves is to block the water supply, and another important resource is gas. It ran through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have just one more question and then I'm one. One more item, this is about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us on Tuesday about what you saw in 1992 and several comments, and I can't really address all of them; for instance, that in April 1992, nothing serious happened. You portrayed, I suggest to you, a fairly one-sided picture of the events in 1992, that the VRS forces and the JNA forces that they didn't shell the city, for instance, causing suffering of the civilians. Are you repeating that today?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the VRS forces in April were not established yet. There were Serb armed guards, and the JNA did not join these forces. Just like in April, there was the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. There were clashes between these Serbian guards and the Patriotic Leagues and the MUP forces. The VRS was not established in April. It became truly operational in a military sense in June 1992. After the disintegration of the JNA between the 3rd and the 9th of September, when the command on Dobrovoljacka Street was attacked, there were clashes between members of the Territorial Defence and the Serb forces. Prior to the departure of the army, I wasn't involved in that and thereafter I joined the VRS. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But you testified about this time-period, and I'm not interested in whether it was the JNA before may 1992 or the VRS after May 1992. But are you saying that, for instance, in May 1992, that JNA or VRS did not shell civilian parts of the city, for instance, Bascarsija? Are you standing by that what you testified on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Had only three shells hit Bascarsija, since these are fragile, small houses built in Turkish style, it would have been completely destroyed and reported all around the world. And not a single of these houses was damaged in the slightest during the war, and you cannot say that this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know a VRS officer called Mirko or Marko Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you certainly know General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do. I have seen him at least ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you hear him talking?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have exhibit 03168. It is an intercept which involves General Ratko Mladic, and he talks specifically about Bascarsija. It dates of 28th May of 1992. So if this exhibit could be played please, it's very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it has a running transcript which show what is it said. There with two speakers: Ratko Mladic and Mirko Vukasinovic, who is a fairly high ranking VRS officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, General Ratko Mladic, he was interested in the barracks. He was interested in firing at Bascarsija, right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can hear here that they should fire at Bascarsija, but that did not happen. I claim with full responsibility, and I am prepared to face the consequences if it proves to be true that Bascarsija was targeted. That was the 25th of May, and the conscripts were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Stop, Witness. I'm stopping you. I'm stopping you because Mr. Tapuskovic has a point to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not hear what date this intercept refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 28th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't have any more questions, Mr. President. Except for the admission of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P750, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 20th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one question of clarification. I can't remember exactly whether it had to do with the Exhibit P42 or whether it was P225 of the 7th of April, 1995, but I'm going to read the contents. In this exhibit -- and we find it back in the transcript, page 12, lines 2 and 3: In the document itself, General Milosevic said to his superior that his troops launched an air bomb of 150 kilos on the Hrasnica centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Judge Mindua, this is P255. You're correct, and it's on page 2 in the middle of -- of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you so much, Mr. Prosecutor. So we're talking about P255. In this document, General Milosevic mentions the launching of a 150 kilogram air bomb on that centre. In the next sentence, mention is made of Muslims who said that a Luna rocket was launched. I don't quite understand. Could you remind me? There is a reference to a 150-kilo bomb here, and what does that mean, and how do you account for the interpretation by the Muslims? I can't put that together.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a huge difference. If you have a 250 kilogram aerial bomb and a Luna rocket which is five to six metres long. It's a huge thing, a huge diameter. And if a Luna had hit, well, this is just some confusion. There would not -- this could not have happened during the cease-fire because we were afraid of air-strikes, reprisals. When we seized four Howitzers because we were afraid there would be an attack, there were NATO air-strikes immediately because of our violation of the exclusion of heavy weapons. And if we had used -- if we had fire add a Luna rocket on such a protected area, then God knows what would have happened. This is either a confusion, errors, or some kind of forecast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But your enemies, they mixed things up, right? I'm Talking about this Luna rocket. But this 150 kilo air bomb, or bomb, was it an air bomb? This 150 kilo air bomb, was it effective launched? Yes or no. And what kind of bomb was it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was not launched, and it was not supposed to be launched. The Muslim forces, their officers, their technical people, on the basis of a piece of an aerial bomb or Luna rocket, draw conclusions as to what actually hit the area. There are experts who are able to determine on the basis of the debris what had impacted there, and they concluded this was a Luna rocket. We didn't have Luna rocket launchers. And if a Luna rocket had hit Hrasnica, half of Hrasnica would be gone. It would have to be destroyed, because it's a huge, huge thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I have one last question. So this was not a Luna missile, but what was it then? Was something actually launched; and if so, what was it, in relation to this report made by General Milosevic to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all orders have to be carried out if there is no need to carry them out, but probably there was an explosion. I didn't see it. Maybe there was a minor explosion that they caused, and then they said it was an aerial bomb, a Luna, whatever. This is really quite unclear. There is a lot of confusion. I know that we would have been blamed for any such attack, any such launching. It would be covered in the media and definitely air-strikes would have followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question, but you're not answering it, so I will continue. I'm not talking about the way the Muslims interpreted the document. I'm talking about the document that was written by General Milosevic. In this document, if this is a real document, he's talking about this 150 kilo bomb. And my question to you is the following: I would like to know what exactly this thing was. You told us it was not a Luna missile. Fine. But was there a 150 kilo bomb? Yes or no. And what nature was it? Either it did not exist, and thus this document is a fake document, and that's what you're saying it is counterfeit, or it did exist and I would like explanations.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This aerial bomb was not launched, that's for sure. And I said already that it was not supposed to be launched. And if it had been launched, then we would have here in front of us a document from the United Nations indicating that we had violated the cease-fire by firing such an a heavy weapon into this inhabited area. So this is my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just have a follow-up question after. I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. So when we return, the question, and then Mr. Tapuskovic, if he wishes to re-examine. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, what is it? Had you a follow-up question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just a clarification on the issue raised by Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one, and I'd like, Witness, to go back to P225, second page: "Our forces," the section you discussed with His Honour Judge Mindua. First of all, it says here, "250 kilograms, AB." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then going back to the initial sentence, it talks about what "our forces" did. Is that correct. It says, "Our forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, where is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's just the title of the second paragraph: "Our forces." Just above the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So here the commander of the corps kind of tells in this combat report his superior command what he did, what the status was of his forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the next sentence, or the first real sentence in second paragraph, talks about a past event. It says: "We responded to enemy fire as follows." It looks back. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then it says, in the second part of that three-followed paragraph, it says that: "In this Ilidza Brigade, one 250-kilogram AB was launched at the centre of Hrasnica." So that is past, that's a fact, that's done. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this, this passage quite well, and I do say that this is what it says here. And it says here that: "According to the information from our audio surveillance officer, Muslims claim that a Luna had hit." I can vouch for the fact that this aerial bomb was not launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veljovic, on the first day of your testimony, perhaps at the very outset, I showed you a document, which is D185.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please have it brought to the screen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that the Prosecutor asked you some questions about this document, too. Do you remember this document? Could you please look at the date on it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your combat report that we've already discussed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Let me just check the signature. Yes, that is what it is. Yes, that's a report that I sent. I was a captain first class at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, the brigade commander, where you served, who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dragomir Milosevic. Colonel Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what is this? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is just a regular combat report sent to the corps command. I don't know whether Siptic or Galic was the commander, perhaps Sladoje was the deputy commander. But every day, in the afternoon or evening, we from the brigade would send our reports to the corps, and then the corps would send its report to the Main Staff of the VRS, and the VRS Main Staff would then inform the ministry and the government, as it is well established system. You get reports from the battalion and then it goes all the up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade it at that time, who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I showed you this document before, and could you please read out item 2, once again.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Units of the brigade, respond only in exceptional circumstances when enemy fire reaches such intensity that it endangers the lives of our soldiers." In other words, we were supposed to open fire only when the intensity of the enemy fire reached such levels that it endangered the lives of our soldiers, and we were not supposed to respond to any minor provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the date of this? 13th September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So at one point you received an order from Mr. Dragomir Milosevic to this effect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So we were not supposed to open fire, respond to the enemy fire, on their soldiers until their fire reached such intensity that it endangered the lives of our soldiers, and only then were we supposed to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what are you reporting here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we probably inform the corps command about our daily activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we sent this to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the commander was close by, and he worked alongside of us, exercising command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notify him that you actually complied -- that you actually did as it is stated here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain this?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the operations organ of the brigade, we collected information from the battalion, and we informed the brigade commander who decided what we're supposed to do and what we are not to do, and he said that fire is to be returned only if there is intense enemy fire. That was the system that was established, and that is how -- that is where we report to our superior command that this was an order that we received from our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then General Milosevic moved to another post; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In February, as I already stated, February 1993, he went to the Drina Corps where he was the chief of the operations and training. And in 1993, in June or July, he came back as the Chief of Staff in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived on the 19th of December, 1994, were his orders in the spirit of this order that he issued at that time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I kept saying throughout my evidence that he always issued such orders. He was always afraid that the troops would not comply with the rules an orders that you were issued, and every time he visited the units he would always warn troops about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, well, you already discussed this issue; but while we're on this document, could you please tell me something about the investigation that was carried out into the death of the civilian. Could you please tell me, what does it mean? When it says "Soping," what is Soping?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well that is part of Grbavica. That was part of our area controlled by the VRS. We informed him that the shell had fallen and there were casualties, and we indicate that a couple of hundreds of metres away that civilian and that the security organs, civilians, and law enforcement agencies were carrying out an investigation. Sometime there would be murders in our areas, and the case would be prosecuted and somebody would be sentenced to maybe ten or 15 years in prison. A Serb would kill a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is the following: Given the circumstances, and in particular during the offensive that you spoke about, could your side have conducted any investigations in the area of responsibility of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's a new subject. We haven't discussed that. He, certainly not in chief, discussed investigations done or not on civilians deaths. In fact, he denied that there were any cases as such. I didn't touch it in my cross-examination because there was no need to. So that is something new which I have to cross-examine again, whether putting issues to him. So I don't think that's something that should be opened right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor says it doesn't arise from his cross-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We agree. It is a new subject. It doesn't arise. Move on to another area, and please remember the purpose of re-examination. It's confined to matters that arise out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, but he did mention this on direct, but I do think that you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In August of 1995, what did you become and when?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said yesterday, in August 1995, I was appointed as the acting commander of the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, which was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You've given me an answer. My question is: Do you remember when it was? You already stated that.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of August and on the 7th of August, I reported that the brigade was combat ready. On the 1st, I took over; and on the 7th, I reported that the brigade was operational so that my commander knew that he could count on this brigade. And on the 7th of August, it was combat ready. It became operational for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was Commander Milosevic on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that as soon as this brigade was established or perhaps sometime earlier, in fact the whole of the month of August, he was absent because he was undergoing treatment. He had an eye problem, so he was undergoing treatment. He returned in -- sometime in mid-September, I think. He returned to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me when did the NATO air-strikes begin in 1995? I'm not referring to the NATO air-strikes in May.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO air-strikes began on the 30th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember when General Milosevic returned in relation to this point in time.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He returned in the second half of September, some -- just before the air-strikes stopped, because the air-strikes lasted for almost a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, in the time-period between December 1994, late December 1994 and April or May 1995, can you describe the situation in terms of combat activities?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The full cease-fire was signed to apply on all front lines between the BH army and the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to now show a document, P744. It's a Prosecution Exhibit. A document originating from the United Nations. It was not translated into B/C/S at the time when it was actually first used in court. At the time when it was shown the -- to the witness, my learned colleague read out this document, and the Defence did not have the B/C/S translation. And I would like to look at item 1 of this document, P744, and I would like to ask the interpreters -- or perhaps I can just show him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the document. The witness doesn't speak English. And since he did tell us that this was a peaceful period, I would like to show him this document so that can he have a look at it. Well, I didn't have the B/C/S version. Could he then have a look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I? No, I can't. It's a little bit -- "Situation in Sarajevo was normal, but tense in the central city/Grbavica area and Sharpstone/Sedrenik. Sarajevo north remains under a complete restriction of movement in their area of responsibility. Zupa remains calm."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you just read Zepa remained calm, but, as you said, the situation was normal in Sarajevo, too?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he mentioned the city centre in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait for me to finish my question. This report, does it indicate that what you have just told us, that the situation was calm, in this period, in December 1994 until February?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been calm. And had there been any such fire from heavy weapons, it would have been a catastrophe. But this report indicates that the situation was normal but tense. I know what I know, but this is what is stated in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, from August 1994 until the end of the conflict, what was the situation like at Spicasta Stijena? What kind of fire was most often exchanged there at Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the area of Grdonj that we talked about yesterday. It was sporadic gun-fire, infantry fire between two warring parties. Nothing more than that. Sporadic, one trench facing another trench. It's 20 or 30 metres. Soldiers from one trench are firing at soldiers in another trench. Nothing more than that. And at that time it was peaceful, but there would always be a random shot of two from infantry weapons, whatever. You would always hear a gunshot, even in peacetime, from a building, from a trench, from wherever on both sides. It would never happen that no shots were heard. You would just hear an occasional rifle fire or whatever. Sometimes it was celebratory gun-fire, but that was the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, geographically, Spicasta Stijena was part of what hill?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hill of Grdonj; that is to say, the feature of the hill of Grdonj. That is near the village of Mrkovic. To the right is the village of Radava, under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please show the witness the photograph that was admitted as P749.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you look at this photograph can you tell us whether at Zlatiste there is a place from which you can see this kind of view of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Editing can do anything nowadays with photograph, but this is not a place at all because the road could be seen right behind the back of this man on the photograph. Also, the picture is narrower so it's not right, and also there is a trench here as if it were dug only yesterday; whereas, as the picture from Spicasta Stijena has some kind of pole. And can you see that nothing was ever done there, and that is what irritates me. Spicasta Stijena has no trench and then also there is an iron post, and you never dig a trench near something that is that prominent. So I can't understand that. And also you can zoom in, zoom out in photography nowadays. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this area. Imagine if something was not taken that way. I mean, perhaps I could not even recognise the place where I was born, the house where I was born, if such a broad view is taken. I mean, I really cannot recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you think that in that sense that is editing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because I see a trench here, and up there I do not see a trench. And, as a matter of fact, I see some kind of trench that was not dug properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is this trench?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In front of this man who is sitting in it, observing something, sitting there. There's this little thing dug in the ground, whatever. The other picture has this pole, this post, and you can see that the land is hundreds of years old. You will see that no trenches were ever dug there, and yesterday the Prosecutor claimed that there was a trench there. And that's why I cannot recognise it properly. And, also, as they zoom in, zoom out, the city itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. But where could this be? What place could this be? What place could this correspond to? If we lock at the zones of responsibility of the two armies, where could this possibly be?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in Sarajevo, there are pits like this and scenery like this everywhere, especially near Trebevic, Grdonj, the river, up there, Sedrenik, and then those settlements up towards Trebevic, parts towards Zlatiste. When you go from Siroka to Debelo Brdo, there are rocks, cliffs, like that, and all sorts of pictures can be taken and you cannot orient yourself. I don't know. I see some bit of wood here, a tiny, little forest, a view towards Kosovo, and in part towards Vogosca, and in this area sort of vis-a-vis Hum, and then Colina Kapa, underneath Colina Kapa, underneath this part here, where Debelo Brdo is, and so on and so forth. However, I cannot say precisely where this is, and tell the Judges this is exactly where this is. That would not be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, out there where you were in Zlatiste, where were the trenches where the army of Republika Srpska was in relation to the road?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trenches were on the road itself, and one road was at the tower that was built by Austria. This is a very big thing. There were three trenches that only had a view of the town: The right bank of Miljacka, the settlement, that is to say, towards Sedrenik, Zuc, Pofalici, Velesici. All of that could be seen, and those areas towards Sedrenik and Grdonj. And parts of Grdonj could be seen from there as well, everything, because Grdonj is on the other side, the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question in relation to this. The place where you were, when this incident occurred, when the bunker was hit, from that place, is there a view of this kind, this kind of view?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this kind. But from that elevation, there is a much better view than from the trenches. 50 per cent better. So it's in our territory way up above the road. Trebevic, when you go up hill at Trebevic, and that's where the view was not a bit better but considerably better. However, trenches were done --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter could not hear the speaker because of the noise coming from the Defence side in that microphone. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last sentence. "However trenches were," and the interpreter didn't hear the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
