utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can the Defence microphone please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He asked me about the observation post of the corps command, and I said it was a well-appointed trench. I said that even the explosion of a projectile could not blow it up. He had a good view, and what I see here in front of me is not that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. I should say that we have spent much more time than was anticipated for this witness. I think seven hours was the time that was estimated, and we are now, I think, into nine hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight hours. Your Honours, I'll hurry up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one question in relation to all of this. Yesterday you said that this position corresponded to the positions of what army?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at all what the place is, where this trench is, and whether this was done there peacetime; or was it just some hole that was found and somebody had his picture taken there, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move quickly through a few documents now that the Prosecutor dealt with in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First P694, Lukovac. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this considerably when answering Mr. Waespi's questions. This first page speaks about positions and the weapons of which army?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, this is a pure military order, and first in the order there's an assessment of the enemy, then our forces, then neighbouring forces, and then a decision is made. The commander and whoever made this deployment first presents what the enemy deployment is, and the first page is the deployment of enemy forces. In order to elaborate an order, you need seven to ten points, so that this would be done properly. And if this is being done for further activities, then first there is an assessment of the enemy in order to position your own forces. First you assess the enemy and then you view your own forces and you see what you're supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he says, "In front of our force defence," then and so on and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is reading out very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, please follow counsel, and don't volunteer information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You saw this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this document. I saw it here and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now when you saw it, this document speaks about what kind of action? Was this action that was envisaged as a large-scale action?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was action that was envisaged on a bit of a larger scale, but it was defensive and then you move into an attack. This was never realised though. That was a preparatory document. And now whether it would be materialised or not, it really on the decision of the commander and the Main Staff, and they never decided and this was never actually entered into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can hear the interpreter gasping for breath because you're speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say that the order is a preparatory document. Whether it will be materialised or not, well, it can just remain as a document stating that it existed. And since this operation was not carried out at all, it is invalid; that is to say, that this operation never took place. We have to look at 100 options; but if we don't carry them through, that is a different matter, and an army makes different documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljovic. Let's try to cut things short if we can. Thank you. And then just one more question in relation to this, and that is: When it was planned, it was planned for what area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was planned for the area of Mount Igman, right here, between the Herzegovina Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, precisely up here. That is what i have been saying, in that back water where there is just ridges and rocks and nothing in the middle of nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last matter that I'd like to deal with. Let's not dwell on it much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P42 is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, this is the document that was shown to you a few moments ago by Mr. Waespi and it pertains to the TV building. I'm not going to go back to that though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a signature here, anybody's signature, a signature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no signature, but it says Commander Major-General Dragomir Milosevic, but we can all see there is no signature there in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I have a final question that comes to my mind because you have been the operations officer and working closely together with General Milosevic, and my question relates to General Milosevic's command over his subordinate forces. And I put this question to you because we have heard evidence during this trial to suggest that General Milosevic was merely carrying out orders that came from General Mladic. So I would like to ask you to describe briefly for us, if you can, the independence of General Milosevic in his command over the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the time when you were working with him as an operations officer. Do you understand me question?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please reply.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milosevic was authorised to command the unit placed under his command by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and to defend. As for assault actions, he only could do that with relation to smaller features. If it involved wider scale operations, he had to seek approval from a superior command. As for other minor things that happened, it was impossible for Mladic to be there on a daily basis and say, "Don't shoot if one company or battalion attacked another." However, if a large-scale operation was launched towards more important features or the town, he was not allowed to do that before reporting to superior officer and seeking an approval for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That was brief and well described. My question to you is then what do you mean by a major operation? Could you give a few examples of what would require the approval of the Supreme Command and also an example of what would not require such approval from above?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, he had the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: His name is Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. He had the right to improve a tactical position only partly. But in order to capture the whole mount of Igman and to endanger a protected area to link up the forces between the west and the east part, he was not allowed to do that without an approval from the Main Staff of the VRS, because that would mean a large-scale undertaking and he had to report to a higher command in order to -- for them to coordinate command and control and be fully informed of what was happening in whole theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would General Milosevic be entitled on his own authority to launch defensive operations in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting. Just one thing about the transcript. "The whole theatre of war," you have to add, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In place of what is written in the transcript on page 51, line 21, you see, what is written was: "What was happening in the whole theatre of war." But the witness said: "The whole theatre of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Mr. Witness, would you please reply to my question: Could General Milosevic, on his own authority, decide to launch a defensive operation within the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My name is Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, he had the right for defence purposes to fortify defence positions as he saw fit and best to arrange for engineering works, to have covers and roads built and constructed, to arrange the deployment of weapons and things as he saw best and fit. He is at the lines reached and he is entitled to do all these works, and he has to report back about what is being done. That is as far as defence is concerned. He is entitled to do all these things, but he cannot move forward. He can only look for some better elevations offering better view and deploy forces in those places in order to get the best possible position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if we look to some of the examples that we have been discussing during your testimony, my question to you would be: Would General Milosevic have to seek approval from the superior command in order to apply or to employ modified air bombs, for instance?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. Most probably he would have to submit a request for these air bombs. But where they were stored and things like that, i don't know that. All I know is that the corps didn't have the air bombs in their depots, where they were, who issued approvals. And I believe it would require an approval from the Main Staff, because this ammunition and some refurbishing probably was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence. This is it how I see it. Given that we did not have in the corps this kind of weapons ever, nor would it ever envisaged per establishment during peacetime, these were bombs to be used by aircraft. How all this went on, I cannot say precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what about orders to initiate sniper attacks? Would that be something that would fall within the authority of General Milosevic, without having to seek approval from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The organisation of firing systems at the positions is done by the squad, regiment, battalion, platoon commanders. This is not at all within the jurisdictions of a commander. These were minor orders. He just issue general orders how to engage target. How the commander of a platoon is going to organise firing position, it didn't concern him. These were a minor point. He cannot be at all places at all times. He was directing global tactics of the corps, together with the staff, and you have subordinate units. Just like in a factory, you have engineers, you have managers, and then you have labourers who do the work, you have draftsmen who prepare blueprints, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let us be concrete just for a moment. Let us assume, just as an example, that sniper fire is to be directed from the Metalka building in Grbavica. Would that be something that would have to require an order from General Milosevic, or could that be initiated without him giving prior approval?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could happen that did he not give an approval, then a platoon commander can issue such an order, but only to engage a military target. He was not allowed to issue orders engaging a civilian target and prepare such positions. But within the company, other commanders would be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand your position on that. Would the platoon commander then have to report back to General Milosevic after the sniping had taken place from, let's say, the Metalka building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So General Milosevic would not subsequently be informed by his subordinates that sniping fire had been launched from this building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wouldn't be informed, because that was a minor operation done by a squad commander targeting an enemy trench. Every unit had its own scope of responsibilities within its area to better organise its positions and undertake actions, because this is such a low level that he wouldn't stoop to that level to tell each and every person what to fire at this. This is not a job for a general to do. This is it something even to be done by group commanders made up of three men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But would an order to launch sniper fire from various parts of SRK-held territory be ordered by General Milosevic? Would he ever be involved in the planning of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, to your colleagues and everyone in the courtroom to the fair treatment you afforded me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your next witness, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness is Milorad Katic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. If I may be allowed to ask the first few questions directly in order to gain time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You can lead on the non-contention introductory matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: My name is Milorad Katic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 26th of January, 1954 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You finished elementary and secondary school in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering in Sarajevo in 1979?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict that existed there found you in the position of the manager of the Pretis factory, or rather, an organisational unit of Pretis, which was called HDM, and that was in Vogosca, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, can you tell the Chamber whether prior to April of 1992, in addition to the job that you were doing, have -- did you have any other social responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that in 1990, at the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was elected deputy for the municipality assembly of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please speak at the corresponding pace, and that we should both bear in mind to observe pauses between questions and answers. Can you tell me what this involved, and how did it look like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I can say that in the territory of Novo Sarajevo municipality, in the Autumn of 1990, at the multi-party elections, Serbian Democratic Party won these elections. The runner-up was the SDP, the Party of Communists; and the third, according to the election results, was the Party of Reformists. In the fourth place was the Party of Democratic Action. In the fifth place was the HDZ Party. And there was another party, I don't remember exactly, which had seats in the assembly of Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can you tell me on what basis was the constituents and the deputies were elected in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: At the time, the city of Sarajevo had between 400 and 500.000 inhabitants, and Novo Sarajevo municipality had approximately 90 to 100.000 inhabitants. I believe that the majority, that is to say 60 to 70 per cent of inhabitants, were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now show you a map that we have had an opportunity to see quite a few times here in this courtroom. And, if possible, I would like you to be given a pen with which you're going to mark on the map the area covered by Novo Sarajevo municipality before any conflicts broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to hand the witness the pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark the entire area covered by Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise, I can't see without my glasses. The municipality of Novo Sarajevo covered these areas, between the new town, Cengic Vila; Dolac Malta; all the way up to the Hum hill, and I can't tell you exactly where the boundary was at the Hum hill. Between these two municipalities, there's the local commune of Velesici, and then it goes down. The boundary then goes down below Marindvor into Kovacici; through Kovacici towards the Vrace, or Miljevici hill; and then behind Miljevici to Stanojovici [phoen] and the village of Petrovici. Well, the village of Petrovici is not depicted here in its entirety. But then from Dolac Malta over the Hrasno hill and the Hrasno neighbourhood; the Mojmilo hill; and then into Lukavica, the Bijelo Bojska [phoen] Road; and then the boundary goes to Trvdemici, the local area commune of Telava. And that would be the area covered by Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please show me the location of your house?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: My house is at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it, and mark Vraca while you're at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I think it's somewhere here. That Would be the Vraca Memorial Park. It's here, and my house is at -- in Ohridska Street, which would be somewhere here. No, no. I made a mistake here. I marked the boundary of the municipality quite inaccurately, because this is really --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, we will have to fix it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will have to fix it because it goes like this, if I may do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, a mistake seems to have been made, and it has to be corrected because this boundary is quite different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very small map. If could you please enlarge it, because this way I really can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a larger version, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's why I say, Your Honours, may I be allowed to make a correction, to correct this line, because really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you asked me where the Vraca Memorial Park was. It's here, and my house is here, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible to erase the previous line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please mark the location of your house with the letter?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please write a large letter C -- in fact, OPS in large letters.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it means, and let's leave it like that, the Novo Sarajevo municipality. And now could you please tell me what ethnic group was in the majority in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: As I have already stated, 60 to 70 per cent of the population in the Novo Sarajevo municipality were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And as for the deputies in the Novo Sarajevo municipal assembly, what was their composition?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I already indicated that the Serbian democratic party was in the lead. I think it had 24 seats; and in the overall municipality, there were 100 seats. And as soon as it won at the 1990 elections -- well, in fact, on the basis of the SDS's victory in the 1990 elections, you can conclude from this fact that the Serbs were in the majority in Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the last time that you went to work in the factory where you were employed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The last time I went to work, I think, it was a Friday, the 2nd of April, or maybe the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in the days that followed? Could you please describe that for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, on that day, I think it was the 3rd of April, when I came home to Vraca with my wife, it was my daughter's birthday on that day, and we prepared the party, the birthday party. That was to take place on the 3rd of April and the 4th of April, the following day, and I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I think you have said enough. Could you please explain to the Judges what did you know at that time about the developments in Sarajevo or, in fact, anywhere in the territory of the country that still existed at that time? Did you get any information? What did you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I followed the media, I watched TV, I read the papers, and I saw, I realised that in 1991 there were conflicts in Slovenia and then also in Croatia. And I can say that in Sarajevo itself, on the 1st of March, 1992, roadblocks were put up, and a Serb guest at a wedding, Nikola Gardovic, was killed in Bascarsija. There were those roadblocks and then there were also conflicts, I think, around Bosanski Brod. I think it was the village of Sijekovac, and then conflicts in Bijeljina and around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I want to know is what was your attitude towards all that? What did you think would happen? How did you feel about it? What did you think would happen in Sarajevo? Did you perhaps believe that the events would take a different course?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I think, and in fact at the time and so did my family, that this was a thing of the past and there would be no conflict in Sarajevo apart from those roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And please, tell me, in the situation and given your job at the time, what were your plans at the time? Did you have any specific plans in your daily life? You have to wait for my question to be recorded in the transcript first, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I got an apartment from my company, the Pretis factory, and I was about to move into this apartment in Sarajevo at that time. And in mid-March, I and my wife, we bought furniture to furnish our apartment and to move into it. It was a new building in Dobrovoljacka Street. That is in the old town municipality, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us where this apartment would had been had not the events not taken course?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, it is a pity that this is such a small scale map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with the letter S.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you finally move into that apartment, in light of the fact that you had already furnished it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I was there for just one day, together with my wife and my two children. We put things in their proper places. My children decide who had would take such room, but I was supposed to move in for good on the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell us what happened? You said that you had the birthday party for your daughter, and what happened? Something that really put a spanner in the works, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, this was on the 4th of April, as I already said. We were sitting outside in the open. The weather was nice, and then there were shots. We heard shots. They were coming from an area further away from the Vraca Memorial Park.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could I please stop you there for a moment. Could you please show us where Vraca is? Could you please mark it with a letter G, but could you please draw a circle around the whole area, so that we get an approximate idea of its size.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: This is the Vraca memorial park, and the clashes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, just a moment. Could you please mark it with letter GG?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The Memorial Park?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The whole area, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please go on. What happened when you heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: When I heard the shots, my neighbours started gathering around the house. It was a spontaneous activity, and they asked me, "What is going on?" Somebody said that there had been some clashes at the police school at Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Clashes involving whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, as we learned, there were some clashes between the police forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you please explain how the police forces were supposed to carry out their tasks. So how, how did those clashes occur?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was to learn later, there had been an internal division inside the police force of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How, in what way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, on the one hand, they wanted to divide the police into the Serbian police of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslim police, if I can give you an answer of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened there at this place where you had all gathered, having heard those shots?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, people started to gather spontaneously and started asking for weapons because they panicked. They were terrified, if I can put it that way. And I can say that after an hour or two, vehicles started coming with weapons. As far as I know -- now, whether they were members of the Territorial Defence or -- well, panic stricken people simply stood in queues by the trucks and they asked for weapons. Among others, I was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone there who did not belong to the Territorial Defence, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: If I can put it this way, it was only territorials who there and people from Vraca, or rather, the neighbouring villages of Miljevici and Petrovici. There won't any members of the other army, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers of the Yugoslav army there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Nowhere were there any members of the Yugoslav People's Army present there, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges now what it was that happened then when you received weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I can explain. First of all, these weapons were fully conserved. On that day, not everybody was armed. These weapons were being distributed over the next three or four days, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll give you an opportunity to explain that as well, if you wish. But who was it that was being armed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: It was only the inhabitants who lived that were being armed, from street, Vraca, Gornji Crevaci, where we lived, the village of Mrkovici, and the rest; that is to say, only the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please draw that line here on this map.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with a R.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were the houses of all these people who were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, our houses were there, at this line that I indicated. That's where we lived, or rather, a bit further this side. If we look at the village of Miljevici or Petrovici and the rest. So it was only the residents of that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll have to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, let us proceed from where we broke of a few minutes ago. Can you tell the Judges what kind of weapons you received on that occasion, when weapons were received?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I can say, as far as weapons were concerned, that all of it were automatic or semi-automatic rifles. We did not receive any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the vicinity of these positions of yours and your houses, did you see any other weapons that were there perhaps at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I have already said that we only got automatic and semi-automatic rifles. I did not see any other weapons. At that time, there weren't any near our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katic. Can you tell me you were there, you got weapons, and how were you then organised? How did things go then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I have already said that we organised ourselves at our own initiative. We immediately appointed a platoon leader. That was my next door neighbour, Ranko Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was he, in terms of profession, when he was chosen commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: He had a forwarding business. He was not even a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said "platoon." How many people there were, can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I can. There were about 30 to 35 of us, in that area, around our houses. We were soldiers, or it was just men, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was it that you wore?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Again, I can say that there was a variety. Some people wore civilian clothes; then there were others who had been reservists, kept some of their military uniforms. So I can say, quite comfortably, there was quite a bit of variety among the then there at the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long was this position that was held by these 30 or so men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: This position was, approximately, about 250 to 300 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now this commander of yours, the former forwarder, how was it that he gave you orders? What kind of orders did he give you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: As for orders of my superior commander, they boiled down to the following: That strictly within 24 hours, we had to be vigilant at our positions, and that no Green Berets or members of the Patriotic League should be allowed to pass there. I knew that these were units that had been formed in the territory of Sarajevo. We had to guard our houses, our homes, our women and children, and our property around our houses. That was the main order issued by our superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were a director in a company, and you had a university diploma of a mechanical engineer. Did you obey these orders that were issued to you by your neighbour who was chosen commander at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, although I had a university diploma as an engineer, I obeyed my commander because I was an ordinary soldier, if I can put it that way. And while I was a soldier, I did not have any other rank. I was just an ordinary soldier, a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you have an opportunity of seeing any other commander who had something to add to these orders at the very beginning, then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: After a few days, I found out that our unit was within the brigade of New Sarajevo, and I met a man who came there as the commander of that brigade. That was the late Budimir Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know who deleted all this from this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has there been a technical glitch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The map will return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They will return. Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Katic, please go on. I interrupted you. You wanted to say something else, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I met commander Budimir Obradovic who was, as I learned, a reserve officer. He had completed the reserve officers' school, and from him I heard an order that was almost identical to the order issued by my platoon leader, Mr. Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: We should not allow any lack of discipline on the line, lest there be an attack coming from the other side, and we had to prevent any destruction in our neighbourhood and any casualties among the women and children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was in the month of April. Tell me, what happened in May, or rather, tell the Judges, not me.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, in the month of May, there were clashes in the territory of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. The major clashes were in the territory of the local commune of Pofalici. That is where my late mother's family lived, and quite a few of my relatives. My uncle and aunt got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. On this map, can you mark Pofalici, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: May I put a circle there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, would you tell me what is the significance of this witness's evidence? What is it leading to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't find this in the indictment now, but the charges are that the JNA was transformed in the army of Republika Srpska. And our witnesses are going to show that there was no transformation at all of the Yugoslavia army, and the witness is going to talk about that, but what happened was the most usual kind of spontaneous self-organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is paragraph 7, where it say, or even before that date, even before the 7th of April, the armed forces that supported the Serbian Democratic Party and elements of the JNA, including units of the 4th Corps, occupied strategic positions in and around Sarajevo. No strategic positions were taken up by this group of people. They simply stood at their own doorsteps, and there was no JNA there and there was no heavy weaponry there. I don't have to explain all of that now, but that is linked up with that. The witnesses, who will testify before you here, will show what it was that happened and how it happened, especially during those first few days, especially in relation to what is charged here, that this happened even before the 7th of April, and that strategic positions were taken. That is something that the Defence has it deal with, in terms of the very beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last sentence in paragraph 7 says, "Much of the bombardment and sniping was from positions in the hills around and overlooking Sarajevo from which the attackers had a clear, detailed, and commanding view of the city and its civilian population." I presume you will also be addressing that, seeking to show that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the key thing that we wish to show through these proceedings, that the army of Republika Srpska was not on the hills at all, except for a few places, and that people in these municipalities -- well, I'm going to bring witnesses here who are going to speak about these municipalities along the lines of which this witness is going to testify as well, or rather, I will question him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said except for a few places. Such as?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That can be problematic when we speak about Trebevic, which was already mentioned, as well as Grdonj and Spicasta Stijena, perhaps Zlatiste, so a few more places. Everything else about 90 per cent of hills around Sarajevo, the Defence will try to prove were held by members of the BH army, and we will discuss where these positions were in several places and whether they provided such an advantage as cited here in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you succeed in that, then you eliminate a major plank in the Prosecution's case. That's my own analysis. We have to wait to see what the evidence will show. Continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours, before proceedings are completed, I never purported to say this happened this way or another. These proceedings should provide answers to the questions and one of the key questions in relation to these developments. We're going to hear from other witnesses, and from this witness I would like to hear something about the position that they had. I came to the point of Pofalici, and if I may continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I said so some time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a circle around this area of Pofalici and tell us what happened there in May?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: In May, in the area of Pofalici, there was, shall I say, a major battle, and since I had quite an few relatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who was involved in this fighting, in this battle?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The battle was between the residents of one part of Pofalici and the then members of the Green Berets or the Patriotic League or I don't know whether they were called the BH army at that time. I said that my uncle and his wife were killed there, Sreto Madjarevic and Dusan Madjarevic; my relative, Slavujka Djurovic, was also killed; Petar Nikola, my relative, who is still missing to this date. And I also later learned there were many, many civilian casualties. From that part of Pofalici, whoever was able to flee, ran away across Zuc hill and went down either to Rajlovac or to Vogosca by crossing the hills. I know that by evicting or expelling Serbs from that area, particularly towards the peak where men Serbian families by the name of Pajdak used to live, everything was abandoned. In June, the entire Zuc hill and the highest elevation in geographic terms, which was Orlic, were taken by the forces of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many people Serb civilians fled from this area to these area areas, Rajlovac, as you said, and so on. How many of them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, about 5.000 residents of that area fled to Rajlovac or Vogosca. Many came via Pale to Lukavica as well. That was the case with some of my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around this whole position captured by the BH army on this map, and can you mark it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I hardly can see the names written on the map, but what I can tell you is that the entire Novo Sarajevo municipality and this part towards Novi Grad municipality was taken over by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: This is this part that can be seen on -- on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But here in the middle of the map, towards the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: This is complete, this part across the Miljacka river, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So was that the situation in May?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Not only this situation prevailed in May, in May and in June --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I am asking you about the situation in May.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: As far as this side is concerned, this is the situation that prevailed in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say at the time - April/May - what happened to the population in other municipalities? You were in this municipality. What was going on there other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that Sarajevo had 400 to 500.000 inhabitants. Out of that number about 150.000 were Serbs. A large number of residents of Sarajevo left Sarajevo in the course of April and May or came to those parts of the city of Sarajevo where the Serbs constituted majority, such as parts of Vogosca, Ilijas, parts of Ilidza, or rather, parts of Novo Sarajevo municipality, Lukavica, Mrkovici, Tilava.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what happened in June? For example, do you know of any other hills that were close to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. In June, clashes broke out between members of the army of Republika Srpska which was established sometime in mid-May. This took place on Mojmilo hill. And, initially, at the beginning of the conflict, there were also members of the Territorial Defence on Mojmilo hill. Just like they were in the part where I was, the families of Milosevic, Majmunovic, and some other families. And in June, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked Mojmilo hill; and then in June, I don't know the exact date, members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over an elevation on Mojmilo hill. I remember that there was a tank there, and that was sort of a key elevation with respect to other parts of Novo Sarajevo municipality. This was one of the most important geographical points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark this hill on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please save this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But before that, let us put a letter M for Mojmilo, and the one up there to be marked with a letter P?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this map to be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay on these positions that you took up together with your neighbours due to the reasons that you explained? How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I stayed at these positions until the 13th of March, 1993, when I was elected president of the then already Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But before that, you said that you were a deputy in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. Where was the municipal hall situated, in which part of the city of Sarajevo? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The municipal hall of Novo Sarajevo or the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo when I was elected, was in the building of the Faculty of Farming and Forestry at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far was it from the Presidency building of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: The Forestry and Farming Faculty was about 300 metres from the residence where Mr. Alija Izetbegovic had his offices, and that is as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But while you were a deputy, and that is prior to the 13th of May -- March, before you were elected president of Novo Sarajevo municipality, did you attend sessions of the assembly or other municipal organs in the period while you were an ordinary deputy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I attended sessions of the assembly of Novo Sarajevo municipality in my capacity of deputy. These sessions were held once a month, or once in two months, so every once and a half months. So over the period of one year, while I was member of the army of Republika Srpska, or less than a year, I attended these sessions of the municipal assembly five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe how it looked like? With respect to the positions that you held, were there any difficulties? How far was it from the place where you were in front of your house? How did you get to the building to attend these sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I always walked. The distance between my house and the municipal hall is about one and a half or two kilometres. I didn't take the main road, which led from Vraca to Grbavica. This is an incoming and outgoing traffic road from Grbavica to Vraca, and it was always exposed to gun-fire from the left and from the right, or rather, if going down towards Grbavica, from high-rise buildings across the Miljacka or from Zuc hill, and on the left, from Mojmilo, or from the direction of Debelo Brdo. For that reason, I most often went to attend these sessions through an area called Basta of the Kovacici water-works, in order to avoid being shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this area that you passed through, is that a populated area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I passed through this area, as I said, that I went through Basta. There were fewer houses at the very exit point of Kovacici, and then I went through the populated area of Grbavica, all the way to the municipal hall building. I have to say that the meetings of the municipal assembly in 1992 were held for the reasons of premises in a elementary school called Sava Kovacevic, which is right next to the faculty building; that is, the Faculty of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to cut the long story short, before you were elects the president of the Novo Sarajevo municipality, what kind of problems there were in the Grbavica area that were discussed before this civilian authority? By that, I mean the Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, it is important to say that as soon as a municipal assembly session is convened, the first item on the agenda is information about the political and security situation. The second item was the distribution of humanitarian aid and whether it is possible to get some of the businesses working again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, were there any other problems related to other issues for affecting the lives of the people there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, before the conflict broke out in that area, there were -- there had been some crimes. Humanitarian aid was not distributed properly. Not all of the population living in Grbavica at the time was taken care of, and because of the discontent that the people expressed following those cases in Grbavica and the crimes that were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of crimes? Could you perhaps explain to the Judges what kind of crimes are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, people often spoke about this group of criminals operating in Grbavica. Their leader was a man by the name of Batko. He was called Batko, as far as I know, and he terrorised primarily the Muslim population. He instilled fear in them and also in the Serbian, among the Serbian population, too. The authorities in the Novo Sarajevo municipality at the time were not really able to protect the population in 1992, the population of Grbavica; and then because many of the deputies in the assembly demanded that, the president of the Novo Sarajevo municipality was removed from office. And on the 13th of March, 1992, there was a session of the municipal assembly; and of the three nominees, I was elected the president by the deputies by majority of votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And some higher political authorities in the Republika Srpska, did they also get involved in those problems, in trying to solve those problems, and did this also affect the decisions made by the deputies?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, the higher ranking officials in Republika Srpska probably did have an interest in what was happening in Grbavica. They received reports from the commissioner, from the people who were the chief commissioners for all the municipalities in the city of Sarajevo, and probably some suggestions were made to remove the officials who were in office in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to turn now to the moment when you actually took up this position, and to deal with some military issues, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a clean copy of the same map that we had on the screen a moment ago. Could we please enlarge this area around Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please first indicate the demarcation lines between the Republika Srpska army and the BH army here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: I will start from Miljacka, the Miljacka river, then there is a street that goes past the Strojrad, and then it follows the Miljacka. This is the Vrbanja bridge. Misko Ivanovic Street should be somewhere here, and here by the Jewish cemetery. That's the Grbavica stadium. Vjelaposka [phoen] Street. So now I'm talking only about the Novo Sarajevo municipality. That's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us Mojmilo on this map, and if you could mark it in the same way that you did on the previous map.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put an M inside this box.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- if at all possible, it might be impossible, could you please mark Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. But Debelo Brdo was in your -- where your positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're not to lead, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I'm not to lead, but this was an obvious error.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, it's physically not like this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the line. I had made a mistake. I don't know if you can accept this, but this here would Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with D. Could you please mark this location with the letter D.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell -- tell us, in what position was the Republika Srpska army, given those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that if you look at this map, you can see that Grbavica was like a kidney, wedged into the city of Sarajevo. It was exposed to fire from Mojmilo hill, or rather, Debelo Brdo hill. And there were some high-rise buildings on the other bank of the Miljacka river, and fire could be opened from there and also from the area above Pofalici, from the Zuc hill, and other elevations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me what was the distance between the two warring sides on this section of the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: If you have the demarcation line in the inhabited area, such as Grbavica, what it means is that on one side of the street VRS troops would be in the houses there, and the BH army troops would be on the other side of the street. So the distance would be maybe 30 metres. That was true for the demarcation line as it ran along the Miljacka river and also if this area here, across Zlatiste, and further on. And there by the road, the distance between the two sides was maybe 30 or 40 metres as you would went to Trebevic, but I didn't mark that on this map because that was another municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please explain to the Court what kind of weapons were available at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: There were infantry weapons in Grbavica, automatic and semi-automatic rifles, and there were three or four armoured personnel carriers. And I can explain right away that those armoured personnel carriers are vehicles mounted with anti-aircraft guns that was 12.7 millimetre in calibre, and there was also a 20-millimetre gun mounted on those vehicles. Those APCs were most commonly used in Grbavica on occasions when somebody was wounded, when some VRS troops would be wounded, or if this also happened to civilians as they ran across a street. So they were used to access the scene and to provide cover against any fire from the opposite side, thus making it possible to give aid to the wounded persons and then to transport those persons to hospital. So as for mortars, Howitzers, tanks, or any other heavy weaponry, there were no such things at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about UNPROFOR? But, first, let me ask you: You know about the total exclusion zone for heavy weapons. You heard about it. We will address this issue later.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at that time, when that happened, did UNPROFOR members demanded the removal of those weapons that you spoke about, or rather, those vehicles, the APCs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Those APCs were not to be moved from Grbavica, but an agreement was reached with the -- with UNPROFOR through the liaison officers from the Republika Srpska army to move those APCs into the alley-ways between buildings or in doorways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you just one more thing: If we look at the whole of the conflict and this situation that you just described to us, the situation at Grbavica, what kind of weapon was most commonly used? So I'm asking you for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, the weapons most commonly used at Grbavica were infantry weapons, automatic or semi-automatic rifles. We also had an UNPROFOR representative in our municipality. He was an expert, and he was able to determine the origin of fire of those sporadic shots that were fired. It was a Norwegian officer, Steiner Bertinusen [phoen]. And in the evening, he would show me that more such bullets had been fired from the other bank of the Miljacka river into the Serbian side than the other way around, from the Serbian side to the other bank of the Miljacka river. And I have to tell you that snipers are mentioned all the time. I know that if you have an automatic rifle or a semi-automatic rifle, if you put on some kind of a sighting device on such a rifle, you can call it a sniper. I can say that I never saw any VRS troops with that kind of weapons at Grbavica. And I often visited the demarcation lines all along Grbavica, and the distance between the two sides at the demarcation line was between 30 and 40 metres. I have to say that I did not see any such weapons on the other side either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was this rifle fire mostly concentrated, if you look at the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the rifle fire in the Grbavica area came from the Debelo Brdo area - that's the area that I didn't draw in properly just a moment ago - and from Mojmilo hill and Hrasno hill, and from the high-rise buildings on the other bank of the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think my time has run out now, and just one more thing. I would like to tender this as a Defence exhibit, this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of June, 2007, at 9.15 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m,
